Article Title: Watch: US strike on vessel kills 4 'narco terrorists' in Caribbean
Article Text:
More than 220 people have died in the US strikes on such vessels in the ⁠Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, Reuters reported.

The US military on Sunday struck a go-fast vessel in the Caribbean Sea, killing four individuals it called "narco-terrorists".The "lethal kinetic" strike was executed by the Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere under the direction of US Southern Command, Southcom said on X."Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking", it said, "The operation killed four narco-terrorists"More than 220 people have died in the US strikes on such vessels in the ⁠Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, Reuters reported.​Since September 2025, the US administration has been targeting such vessels over allegations of smuggling narcotics in the country.In 2025, the Associated Press reported a Trump administration memo saying the US was in an "armed conflict" with the drug cartels.“The President determined that the United States is in a non-international armed conflict with these designated terrorist organizations,” the memo says. Trump directed the Pentagon to “conduct operations against them pursuant to the law of armed conflict,” the memo said, according to AP.“The United States has now reached a critical point where we must use force in self-defense and defense of others against the ongoing attacks by these designated terrorist organizations,” it said.However, the legality of such strikes has been questioned by experts and rights advocates in the US and abroad.Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and a number of independent UN experts have condemned the strikes as unlawful extrajudicial killings.Ben Saul, the UN special rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism, said there are "reasonable grounds to believe" the attacks amount to crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law. Reuters reported.The American Civil Liberties Union has also rejected the Trump administration's justifications for targeting these individuals, calling them "unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims."
Article Summary: The US military on Sunday struck a go-fast vessel in the Caribbean Sea, killing four individuals it called "narco-terrorists" More than 220 people have died in the US strikes on such vessels in the ⁠Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, Reuters reported.

Article Title: In 1931, a Denver Tudor Revival estate was built for $38,000; the 10,000-sq-ft home later owned by jeweler Tom Shane is now the city’s second-most expensive listing at $10.75 million
Article Text:
The property at 575 Circle Drive covers about 10,370 square feet and sits on roughly three-quarters of an acre in Denver’s Country Club neighbourhood (Image Credit: Sotheby's International Realty)

A house built in 1931

Architect Henry S. Koch designed the house in the Tudor Revival style, which was popular in the United States during the early 20th century (Image Credit: Sotheby's International Realty)

Its connection to Tom Shane

More than 10,000 square feet inside

The kitchen opens towards the outdoor spaces, making the transition between the house and garden more practical for gatherings (Image Credit: Sotheby's International Realty)

The garden is a major part of the property

From $38,000 to $10.75 million

A Denver house that cost $38,000 to build in 1931 is now on the market for $10.75 million. The nearly century-old Tudor Revival estate has also had some well-known owners, including jeweller Tom Shane, and remains one of the most expensive homes currently listed in the city. According to Realtor.com, the property at 575 Circle Drive covers about 10,370 square feet and sits on roughly three-quarters of an acre in Denver’s Country Club neighbourhood. Much of what makes the house stand out, though, is not its price. Its original Tudor details, generous spaces, mature gardens and long history have helped it remain a distinctive property in a city where luxury homes continue to command high prices.The estate was built for Mason and Dorothy Lewis in 1931, at a reported cost of $38,000. Architect Henry S. Koch designed the house in the Tudor Revival style, which was popular in the United States during the early 20th century. From the outside, the home has the features expected of the style, including brick and masonry walls, limestone details, half-timbering, leaded windows and large chimneys. Inside, the design continues with detailed woodwork, mouldings and other period features.The house was not built as a modest family home. It was intended to be a substantial residence, and its scale is still apparent nearly 100 years later. Mason Lewis was a Denver lawyer and the son of Robert E. Lewis, who served as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit. The property remained with the Lewis family for around 30 years before changing hands.The estate later became associated with the Gallagher family, who carried out changes to the property over the years. Among those changes were additions above the garage and renovations to parts of the house. Jeweller Tom Shane, founder of the Shane Co. jewellery chain, was another owner of the property. His ownership gives the house a familiar name in addition to its architectural history.Even with changes made over the decades, many of the original features have survived. The residence still has hand-carved limestone, leaded glass and substantial wood detailing. The property is also within Denver’s Country Club neighbourhood, which was designated a historic district in 1990. That historic designation is part of what makes the home different from a newly built luxury property. Its character comes from details that have been part of the house for generations.According to the property listing by LIV Sotheby’s International Realty, the home has about 10,370 square feet of living space, six bedrooms and 7.5 bathrooms. The second floor contains five bedrooms, each with its own en-suite bathroom. There is also a private suite on the third floor that can be used for staff, a nanny or extended family.The lower level is geared more towards recreation. It includes a large gathering space, a kitchenette, gym, sauna and temperature-controlled wine cellar. The main floor has several formal entertaining areas, including a large salon with a fireplace. The kitchen opens towards the outdoor spaces, making the transition between the house and garden more practical for gatherings.For a home in central Denver, the amount of private outdoor space is another significant feature. The estate occupies roughly three-quarters of an acre and is surrounded by mature landscaping. The grounds include rose gardens, a pergola, brick patios and a firepit. There is also an outdoor grilling area.The landscaping helps give the property a more secluded feel, despite its location in one of Denver’s established neighbourhoods. The house is close to Cherry Creek North, with its shops and restaurants, while downtown Denver is only a short drive away. That combination of privacy and access is one reason the property occupies a notable position in the city's high-end housing market.The biggest talking point, however, is the change in price. When the Tudor Revival home was built in 1931, it cost $38,000. Nearly 95 years later, it is being offered for $10.75 million. Realtor.com has described it as Denver’s second-most expensive listing at the time of its report. The increase cannot be explained simply by the age of the house. The property has a large lot, a substantial amount of living space and a location in one of Denver’s established historic neighbourhoods. It also retains architectural details that would be difficult to reproduce in a new construction project.For buyers looking at homes at this level, those details can matter as much as the number of bedrooms or the size of the house. The 575 Circle Drive estate is therefore selling more than space. It offers a house that has been part of Denver’s residential landscape since 1931, has passed through several notable ownerships and still carries much of the character with which it was built. Its current $10.75 million price tag shows just how far the value of the property has travelled from the $38,000 paid to build it nearly a century ago.
Article Summary: The property at 575 Circle Drive covers about 10,370 square feet and sits on roughly three-quarters of an acre in Denver’s Country Club neighbourhood. Architect Henry S. Koch designed the house in the Tudor Revival style, which was popular in the United States during the early 20th century. The estate was built for Mason and Dorothy Lewis in 1931, at a reported cost of $38,000. Jeweller Tom Shane, founder of the Shane Co. jewellery chain, was another owner of the property.

Article Title: Kelowna grower Jordan Abbate’s giant pumpkin weighed 1,485 pounds at British Columbia’s 2026 contest, beating the 1,484-pound runner-up by just 1 pound after six months of daily care
Article Text:
Abbate said he spent several hours each day looking after the plant (Giant Pumpkins British Columbia photo)

A global competition

Working with the pumpkin for 6 months

The organisation holds about 800 competitions around the world each year.

Kelowna grower friend wins too

Bigger Pumpkin next year?

A giant pumpkin grown by Kelowna resident Jordan Abbate won the 2026 B C Giant Pumpkin Contest in Langley, on Saturday, with just one pound separating the top two entries. Abbate’s pumpkin weighed 1,485 pounds, while Team Halliday’s entry came in at 1,484 pounds.The contest was held at Krause Berry Farm in Langley. According to Castanet, Abbate’s win was also a first for the B C Interior, as no grower from the region had previously won the event in its 13-year history.The winning pumpkin was the result of about six months of regular care. Abbate said he spent several hours each day looking after the plant, including watering, pruning and caring for the soil. The work continued even through winter as he prepared the soil for the growing season.Abbate, however, was not very confident about winning before the weigh-off. After learning that his pumpkin had taken first place, he said he was "very satisfied".The B C Giant Pumpkin Contest is the only competition in British Columbia sanctioned by the Great Pumpkin Commonwealth, an international organisation that sets rules and standards for growing giant pumpkins and other oversized fruit and vegetables.The organisation holds about 800 competitions around the world each year. The 2026 event was the 13th B C competition.Contest host Jeff Pelletier had predicted that the scale of the event could lead to records being challenged. "The event gets better every year, and the scale is getting bigger. I believe several B C records will be challenged today, and some may even be broken," he said before the weigh-off, as quoted by Sing Tao Canada Dushi.True to his words, some records were broken during the competition. Although Abbate’s 1,485-pound pumpkin did not set a new B C record, a 1,149-pound giant squash established a new provincial record in its category. Meanwhile, a long gourd measuring 131.5 inches also set a new B C record.The Great Pumpkin Commonwealth recognises eight record categories including giant pumpkin, giant squash, field pumpkin, long gourd, bushel gourd, tomato, watermelon and giant zucchini.Growing a pumpkin to this size requires regular attention over a long period. Abbate said he spent several hours every day taking care of the plant during the six-month growing period."It took many months of watering, pruning and taking care of the plant. Even when winter came, I was still working on the soil," he said.The work does not end once the pumpkin begins growing rapidly. According to Pelletier, giant pumpkins need to be checked almost every day during their fastest growth period.They can also gain weight at a remarkable rate. Pelletier said a giant pumpkin can add up to 60 pounds in one day during this stage. "This growth rate will continue for two weeks. For the six months you grow it, it is like your pet," Pelletier said.That rapid increase in size also creates practical challenges. Giant pumpkins and squash can become so heavy that moving them to a weigh-off requires lifting straps and forklifts. For Abbate, the months of work did bear a sweet fruit.Abbate was not the only Kelowna grower at the event. His friend and fellow Kelowna resident Cassidy Murrell also competed, finishing 10th with a pumpkin weighing 756 pounds.Murrell began growing giant pumpkins about four years ago. He described the hobby as an everyday activity that can take several hours of work.“It’s pretty much an every day hobby,” he said. “I spend at least an hour, maybe even two or three hours a day in the patch. That’s doing everything from pruning to training vines, spraying, fertilizing, checking irrigation, checking on the pumpkin, fighting off the vermin,” Murrell added.The process also involves research before the seeds are even planted. Growers look for seeds with particular lineages, some of which date back to the 1970s and 1980s.Murrell said growers study the history of those lineages to identify traits they want in their pumpkins, including colour and density. They also consider whether a particular lineage is more likely to split.“We use that to determine favourable traits, whether its colour or whether they tend to be denser than other pumpkins. If one lineage tends to split more than others, then we’ll avoid that one. It’s so extensive it’s almost difficult to explain,” he said.Murrell’s interest in growing giant pumpkins began with his family’s tradition of hosting large Halloween parties. His parents later gave him a gift basket containing a seed-starting tray made by his father. That became the starting point for his own giant-pumpkin hobby.He eventually grew a 70-pound pumpkin and took it to a weigh-off. There, he met Abbate and saw Abbate’s much larger 1,090-pound pumpkin.“I grew a 70 pound pumpkin that I was super proud of, took it to a weigh-off, and that’s when I met Jordan Abbate, with his 1090 pound pumpkin that dwarfed my little 70 pounder,” Murrell said.Murrell now hopes to challenge his friend for the title at Krause Berry Farm. He even supplied Abbate with a seedling this year, turning their friendly competition into another reason to watch next year’s contest. “I gave him his seedling this year, so he better watch out next year,” he joked.Last year, Leif Palmberg and his son Victor from Galiano Island, BC, were placed 1st with their 1,758 pound Giant Atlantic Pumpkin.
Article Summary: A giant pumpkin grown by Kelowna resident Jordan Abbate won the 2026 B C Giant Pumpkin Contest in Langley, on Saturday. His pumpkin weighed 1,485 pounds, while Team Halliday’s entry came in at 1,484 pounds. Growing a pumpkin to this size requires regular attention over a long period.

Article Title: Flydubai co-pilot likely acted alone; Israeli probe finds no terror link for now - report
Article Text:
Hamam al-Hammami, the accused co-pilot in the flydubai incident (Image source: LinkedIn)

Corriere della Sera

What happened inside the cockpit

Questions over his past

New reports suggest that the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and trying to seize control of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv probably acted alone.An Israeli official told CNN that information gathered during the investigation so far suggested Hamam al-Hammami acted alone. Another Israeli source said Israel had found no known link between the suspect and any group or government, while stressing that the investigation was still ongoing.The development comes as investigators examine whether al-Hammami made a further attempt to bring down the Boeing 737 after his initial attack on Captain Smit Machchhar failed. An investigation by Italian newspaper, cited by Ynet News, said investigators were examining whether the co-pilot moved the aircraft's two engine fuel switches from “Run” to “Cutoff” after taking control of the plane.According to the report, al-Hammami allegedly pushed the aircraft into a steep descent after disabling the autopilot, potentially attempting to crash it in the Saudi desert after passengers and crew began thwarting his attempt to seize the aircraft.The incident took place on September 30 aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar with a cockpit crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft.Despite being wounded, Machchhar managed to activate the mechanism that opened the cockpit door, allowing cabin crew and passengers to enter and help subdue the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.The UAE attorney general has described the incident as an attempted “terrorist act”. Investigations are being conducted by authorities in the UAE, Israel and Saudi Arabia.US president Donald Trump had earlier suggested that al-Hammami could be linked to Iran, saying it was “based on what I’m hearing”. He did not provide details. Israeli sources now say they have not identified a link to any group or government, although the investigation has not concluded.Al-Hammami, 29, is an Omani national who had previously worked for Oman Air. According to CNN, he was removed from his previous job after concerns about his extremist views. He later joined Flydubai and had been working there for around eight months.Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has separately said al-Hammami had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”, based on information gathered during questioning. He did not provide further details.The investigation has also raised questions over aviation security and the vetting of foreign flight crews.CNN reported that the names of all passengers and crew had been provided to Israeli authorities before the flight took off. Israel's tax authority confirmed receiving the list, but the transportation ministry said its protocols did not include checking the names of flight crew members.The issue is particularly sensitive because Oman does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Netanyahu has said Israel had longstanding arrangements aimed at preventing pilots from countries without diplomatic ties from flying into the country and described the case as exposing a “loophole”.Israel has since ordered a review of security procedures for foreign civil aviation following the incident.
Article Summary: Hamam al-Hammami is accused of attacking the captain and trying to seize control of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv. Israeli sources say they have not identified a link to any group or government, although the investigation has not concluded.

Article Title: No classes in 500 schools on Monday: Why are France students protesting
Article Text:
French riot police were deployed to the manage the protests on Friday

What are students demanding

France is set to partially or completely close up to 500 high schools on Monday as days of student protests over poor education standards have escalated into clashes, vandalism and mass arrests, forcing authorities to raise security concerns.According to the BBC, French education minister Édouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools because security conditions had not been fulfilled.Geffray also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the protests began and that 78 education staff members had been wounded.The protests, which began last week, have spread from Paris to cities including Toulouse, Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.Students and other demonstrators are protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school buildings and a lack of resources.The unrest has triggered a major police response. French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests, while Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 1,747 people were arrested on Friday, according to the BBC.At the heart of the protests are demands for more teachers, including substitute staff, as students complain that teacher shortages are disrupting classes and affecting the quality of education.Reuters has independently identified teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school infrastructure among the main grievances driving the movement.Students are also calling for more resources for schools and better learning conditions. They have raised concerns over overcrowded classrooms and poorly maintained school buildings, with protesters arguing that inadequate infrastructure is making it harder for students to learn.The demonstrations have since escalated into violent clashes in several cities, with protesters confronting riot police and some schools being damaged or ransacked. Reuters has reported arson, attacks on police and widespread arrests as the unrest has spread across France.The government has responded by promising measures to improve school facilities and ensure classes continue, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has also pledged changes to the organisation of school days and greater transparency in the university admissions system.
Article Summary: French education minister Édouard Geffray said lessons would be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools. 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the protests began and 78 education staff members had been wounded. Protests have spread from Paris to Toulouse, Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.

Article Title: How flydubai security failure, across 3 countries, almost led to 'Israel’s 9/11’
Article Text:
File photo: A flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport

Oman flagged him, but the warning did not travel

Hammam al-Hammami

Israel had his name, and still let him fly

The cockpit attack

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for improving airline security? Cross-Border Intelligence Sharing Stronger Background Checks for Crew Better Security Checks at Airports Stronger Cockpit Security & Access Control 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A string of security failures across Oman, the UAE and Israel allowed the flydubai co-pilot to get into the cockpit, a Wall Street Journal investigation has found. The lapses nearly led to an aviation disaster reminiscent of 9/11, despite authorities having reasons to be concerned about him.The failures began in Oman, where authorities had scrutinised Hamam al-Hammami’s online activity and found he showed too much interest in radical ideology to be trusted as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalisation programme and moved him to a desk job, but did not broadly communicate their concerns about him.When al-Hammami joined flydubai in February, the airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience, the WSJ reported. It conducted a criminal-background check, but the earlier concerns that had led Oman to remove him from flying were not passed on to the new employer. The operator, flydubai, later assigned him to the sensitive Tel Aviv route, which he flew multiple times.Oman’s handling of the case also created another missed opportunity. People familiar with the matter said that had the country formally withdrawn al-Hammami’s pilot licence over its concerns, the action would likely have been flagged to the UAE.Instead, the concerns about his extremism were not communicated more widely.The final layer of failures came in Israel, where foreign airlines are required to submit passenger and crew lists before arriving.Airline operator flydubai had submitted the manifest for Flight 1073, but Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews. The ministry also said it had never asked to access a database created in 2023 to help authorised agencies review passenger and crew information because it did not know the database was operational or that it could use it.There was an even more basic warning that should have stopped al-Hammami from flying to Israel. Pilots from countries such as Oman, which does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, are barred from flying to the country. Yet al-Hammami was allowed onto the Tel Aviv-bound flight.Israel’s own previous warnings also raise questions about how the system failed. A classified May 2024 report by the country’s comptroller general had warned that aviation security had grown lax, with fragmented responsibilities and unclear lines of authority. The report also identified manpower and budget problems affecting oversight by the transportation ministry.The security failures culminated halfway through Flight 1073, when al-Hammami attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe after excusing himself to pray.The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to enter and overpower the co-pilot. They then helped pull the aircraft out of a dangerous dive.The UAE’s attorney general has described the incident as an attempted terrorist act. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel suspect al-Hammami was trying to crash the aircraft in Tel Aviv, according to people familiar with their thinking. All three countries are investigating whether he acted alone; so far, investigators have not found links to a foreign power or major terrorist organisation, those people said.The incident has since prompted Israel to review the security of foreign airline flights to the country.
Article Summary: Oman Air banned Hamam al-Hammami from flying, but did not communicate concerns about him to flydubai. The airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience. Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews.

Article Title: Kristin Davis helped rescue one-year-old elephant after finding her alone in Kenya; years later, Chaimu returned to the wild and inspired a sculpture
Article Text:
Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

Kristin Davis helps rescue an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya

From the nursery to Tsavo East: Chaimu learns life among wild elephants

PC: Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

A 2011 Kenya visit strengthens Davis’s ties to elephant conservation

A longer commitment to wildlife conservation

Chaimu becomes part of a larger conservation project

From an orphaned calf to life in the wild

In 2009, a holiday in Kenya brought actress Kristin Davis into an unexpected encounter with an abandoned elephant calf. While staying in the Chyulu Hills, Davis and staff from Kampi Ya Kanzi came across the young elephant on its own. When the calf was still without its mother several days later, a decision was made to intervene. The orphan, later named Chaimu, was about a year old and was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, now known as the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Sixteen years on, Chaimu has become part of a very different story. After years of rehabilitation and time learning alongside wild elephants, she has returned to the wild.Davis was holidaying in the Chyulu Hills when she and people working at Kampi Ya Kanzi spotted the calf. At first, there was uncertainty over whether the elephant had simply become separated from its herd. But the situation did not change over the following days.With the calf continuing to remain alone, the group decided that intervention was necessary. The DSWT was contacted and arrangements were made to rescue the young elephant.She was named Chaimu and, at roughly one year old, began a rehabilitation process that would eventually take her from the Nairobi Nursery to the organisation’s reintegration programme in Tsavo East.Chaimu’s care did not end with her arrival at the Nairobi Nursery. Orphaned elephants in rehabilitation need to develop many of the behaviours they would ordinarily learn from their families, including how to interact with other elephants and function within a herd.After graduating from the nursery, Chaimu moved to the Ithumba Reintegration Centre in Tsavo East. The centre allows older orphan elephants to spend increasing amounts of time around wild elephants before making the transition away from human care.That process was reflected in Davis’s later descriptions of Chaimu. The elephant was regularly mixing with wild herds and learning the skills needed for life outside the sanctuary system.The encounter did not become an isolated episode in Davis’s life. She continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.Her involvement included visits to Kenya. In July 2011, she returned with her friend Ame and filmmaker Roz Edwards, spending time at the Nairobi Nursery before travelling to Ithumba in Tsavo East. During that visit, she stayed at Ithumba Camp, which had been established alongside the reintegration centre and was intended to support limited responsible tourism in the northern part of Tsavo East.Davis also spoke publicly about Chaimu and the charity’s work, including an appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show. She has continued to identify elephant conservation and the illegal ivory trade among the issues she has highlighted.Davis’s work with elephants has since extended beyond her connection with Chaimu. She also served as a Goodwill Ambassador for UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, in 2017, according to The UN Refugee Agency.Her interest in conservation has also crossed into film. The Perfect World Foundation Award says that in 2014, she executive produced and financed Gardeners of Eden, a documentary about the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust and its efforts to protect elephants. The film received recognition at several film festivals, including the Elephant Hero Award at the UN-sponsored International Elephant Film Festival in 2016, and was later a finalist for a Peabody Award.In September 2023, Davis received The Perfect World Foundation Award for her contribution to raising awareness around wildlife and biodiversity conservation.Years after the original rescue, Chaimu’s story became connected to The Great Elephant Migration, a conservation art project involving a travelling collection of elephant sculptures. Davis has supported the project and said she wanted to help raise awareness and funds for conservation work.A sculpture representing Chaimu is part of the migrating herd. Its inclusion links the animal Davis encountered as an orphaned calf in Kenya with the elephant she later saw progressing through rehabilitation and towards life in the wild.By then, Chaimu was 16 years old and had been reintegrated into the wild. Her story therefore spans much more than the original rescue. It covers the long period between being found alone in the Chyulu Hills and eventually becoming capable of living beyond the protection of the rehabilitation programme.Chaimu’s journey illustrates the lengthy nature of elephant rehabilitation. The rescue itself happened quickly once it became clear that the calf was not being reunited with her herd, but the process that followed took years.From the Nairobi Nursery to Ithumba, Chaimu gradually spent more time in an environment where wild elephants could provide experiences and social interactions that a young orphan would otherwise have gained from its family. Her eventual return to the wild marked the later stage of that process.For Davis, the connection began with an encounter during a Kenyan holiday in 2009. More than a decade later, Chaimu’s name remains attached to her conservation work, this time through a sculpture travelling with The Great Elephant Migration and representing an elephant that survived the loss of its original herd and went on to rejoin wild elephants.
Article Summary: Kristin Davis came across an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya in 2009. The calf, later named Chaimu, was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Davis continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.

Article Title: In 2011, a Wyoming couple built a 1,500-sq-ft off-grid home from 1,343 tyres on 55 acres, adding a 66-foot greenhouse, solar panels and rainwater systems; 15 years later, the unusual Earthship is list
Article Text:
The unusual home borders 280 acres of Bureau of Land Management land and is located about an hour north of Cheyenne

Home built as a retreat

Built with 1,343 pounded tyres, the home features plaster walls, bottle-glass work and bottle lighting.

Tyres and bottle glass use

A home in Wyoming built from 1,343 pounded tyres is now on the market for $625,000. The two-bedroom off-grid Earthship was built by its original owners in 2011 and sits on 55.13 acres in Wheatland, near the foothills of Laramie Peak.As per Realtor.com, the 1,500-square-foot home was designed around systems that allow it to operate off the grid. It has a solar array, wind turbine, roof water catchment system, passive geothermal cooling, a backup diesel generator and other backup systems. The property also includes a 66-foot greenhouse.The unusual home borders 280 acres of Bureau of Land Management land and is located about an hour north of Cheyenne. Its construction uses 1,343 pounded tyres, while the interiors include hand-trowelled plaster walls, custom bottle-glass work and bottle lighting.One of the features highlighted by the listing agent is the home's ability to maintain temperatures between 62 degrees and 82 degrees despite Wyoming's conditions."One of the coolest things about the home is that it is at a higher elevation and able to sustain a temperature that never gets below 62 degrees in the winter and 82 degrees in the summer," says Rowan Bennett, who is co-listing the property with Holly Allison of #1 Properties Ranch and Recreation.The sellers are the original owners and built the Earthship in 2011. According to Bennett, they have used it as a secondary residence and retreat rather than as their main home."It has been used as a secondary residence by the sellers, who used it as a retreat. It would also be cool to use it as an investment property and put some yurts on the property," she says.The property is designed to provide several independent systems rather than depending on just one source for its needs. It has solar power, a wind turbine and a backup diesel generator. A roof water catchment system is also part of the home.The systems have backups as well. Bennett said this was another feature that made the property unusual. "What is also unique is that every system has a backup operation, so if the hot water heater goes out, there is a propane backup," she says.The home also has a permitted domestic well. Outbuildings on the property provide additional storage space.The Earthship's walls and design are among its most distinctive features. The residence was built using 1,343 pounded tyres, while bottle-glass work has been incorporated into parts of the home.Inside, the 1,500-square-foot residence has hand-trowelled plaster walls, custom bottle lighting and a built-in bed. It also has flagstone and crushed-shell brick floors, peeled log vigas across the ceilings, and glass doors and walls.The kitchen has custom pine cabinetry with hand-carved diamond inlays. It also features tile countertops and a decorative tile backsplash. The kitchen appliances include a Sun Frost energy-efficient refrigerator and a countertop ice maker. The bathroom has a claw-foot soaking tub and a shower combination with an air massage system.The home is not only built for off-grid living but also includes space and infrastructure for possible future additions. A level building pad on the property has already been plumbed for sewer and is waiting for a future garage or second dwelling, subject to applicable approvals. Water utility has also been stubbed across the road. The space is ready for a possible future pond or garden.
Article Summary: The Earthship was built by its original owners in 2011 and sits on 55.13 acres in Wheatland, near the foothills of Laramie Peak. It has a solar array, wind turbine, roof water catchment system, passive geothermal cooling, a backup diesel generator and other backup systems. The property also includes a 66-foot greenhouse.

Article Title: Federal prosecutors say a Louisiana group rented homes, insured them and caused about 13 residential fires between 2019 and 2026, then filed claims for fabricated losses; seven people have now been ch
Article Text:
​All seven defendants face wire fraud and arson-related federal charges. (FBI photo)

Seven people face federal charges

AI helps identify fraud

Fires part of a years-long scheme

Federal prosecutors in Louisiana charged seven people on Tuesday, in an alleged insurance fraud and arson scheme involving about 13 residential fires between 2019 and 2026. Authorities say the group rented homes, obtained insurance policies and then allegedly caused fires at the properties before seeking money through fraudulent insurance claims.The charges were announced by US Attorney Zachary A Keller for the Western District of Louisiana. According to the official information, the defendants include Lashaundalyn Whitlock Brown, 41, of West Monroe; LaQuadra Whitlock, 26, of West Monroe; Latricia Whitlock, 20, of Monroe; Romenique Whitlock, 37, of Monroe; Jonika James, 25, of Monroe; Iesha Alexander, 26, of Monroe; and Travericka Williams, 27, of Dallas, Texas.According to the indictment, the alleged scheme took place in the Monroe and West Monroe areas. Prosecutors say the defendants rented homes in their own names or through several other co-conspirators and used fraudulent identities to obtain insurance coverage for the residences. They then allegedly set fire to the properties and submitted insurance claims for losses that did not actually occur.Morover, the group also allegedly submitted fraudulent disaster relief claims to a national humanitarian organisation and received cash payments meant for fire victims.All seven defendants have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and use of fire to commit a federal felony. Lashaundalyn Whitlock Brown, LaQuadra Whitlock and Latricia Whitlock also face charges of conspiracy to commit money laundering, concealment money laundering and structuring.The defendants were arrested on September 23, according to the US Attorney’s Office. If convicted on all charges, they could face decades in federal prison, along with substantial mandatory minimum sentences.Prosecutors allege that insurance claims submitted after the fires sought payments for fabricated personal property losses and extended-stay hotel reimbursements. Realtor.com reported that some of the claims allegedly contained identical entries and repeated spelling errors.The allegations also include the use of fraudulent identities when obtaining renters insurance for some of the properties. Authorities say the fires placed firefighters and people living nearby at risk.“The audacity, the recklessness, and the greed of these defendants to allegedly turn fire setting into a for-profit operation is staggering,” Keller said. “The conspirators charged here fed their greed by putting innocent lives at risk, including those of first responders, and destroyed the hard earned property of others while contributing to higher insurance costs for us all,” he added.The case was investigated by the FBI, the Louisiana State Fire Marshal, the Monroe Fire Department and the Louisiana State Police.FBI New Orleans Special Agent in Charge Jonathan Tapp said the alleged scheme affects more than the people directly involved in the insurance claims.“The cost to Louisiana policyholders is impossible to calculate. But every single one of us pays the price when criminals take advantage of programs meant to help actual victims. There is also real damage done to the businesses who invest in our communities,” Tapp said.At a press conference in Ouachita Parish, Deputy Commissioner for the Office of Insurance Fraud Dominique Jones said the Louisiana Department of Investigation used an AI-powered tool called Anti-Fraud One to help identify suspicious claims. Jones said the tool helped investigators uncover organized fraud that might otherwise go undetected.The federal charges also cover alleged money laundering activity. Prosecutors say the money obtained through the alleged scheme was handled through transactions that led to the additional money laundering and structuring charges against three of the defendants.The indictment describes the alleged activity as a years-long conspiracy involving intentionally set residential fires, fraudulent insurance claims and fraudulent disaster relief claims.In court filings, prosecutors also argued that Lashaundalyn Whitlock Brown should remain in custody while awaiting trial, citing a long criminal history from age 17 to her current age of 40. Prosecutors said she was also paroled in 2021 and appears to have begun the subject conduct right after.
Article Summary: Seven people face federal charges in alleged insurance fraud and arson scheme. Authorities say the group rented homes, obtained insurance policies and then allegedly caused fires at the properties before seeking money through fraudulent insurance claims. If convicted on all charges, they could face decades in federal prison, along with substantial mandatory minimum sentences.

Article Title: A Texas man used this Civil War relic as a paperweight for years; bomb experts later found it was actually a live explosive
Article Text:
The Civil War-era shell sat on a Texas man's desk for years as a conversation piece. (Atascosa County Sheriff's Office)

How a Texas man turned a Civil War relic into a paperweight

Experts identified it as a live Parrott round

A Parrott rifle, the Civil War-era cannon designed by Robert Parker Parrott.

The shell was designed for a powerful Civil War cannon

Parrott rifles changed Civil War artillery

The 160-year-old explosive was finally destroyed

A Texas man kept a Civil War-era artillery shell on his desk for years, believing it was nothing more than a harmless dummy round. The object had become a conversation piece in his home, with visitors regularly picking it up and examining it. That changed after a man with military experience saw the relic and warned that it could still be live. The owner then contacted the Atascosa County Sheriff's Office, which brought in an explosive ordnance disposal team from Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland. Experts examined the roughly 20-pound object and identified it as a live Parrott round. It was later transported to an explosives range at Camp Bullis, where specialists safely destroyed it.The man, identified as Steve Martin, had acquired the object from his son, who had found it while fishing. Martin believed it was a dummy projectile and eventually began using it as a paperweight at his home in Atascosa County. For years, the unusual object attracted the attention of visitors, who would pick it up and look at it. Martin said he and others assumed it was some type of inert military display item. That belief remained unchanged until a truck driver with a military background visited and examined the object.The visitor became concerned that its appearance was consistent with a genuine artillery projectile and warned Martin that it might still contain an explosive charge.After receiving the warning, Martin contacted the Atascosa County Sheriff's Office and reported that he might have a live Civil War-era explosive. Deputies arranged for an explosive ordnance disposal team from Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland to examine the object. Specialists confirmed that it was a live Parrott round, meaning the projectile was still capable of functioning as an explosive weapon despite being more than 160 years old. The discovery prompted authorities to treat the object as hazardous rather than as an ordinary historical artefact. Officials said no one was injured during the response and no charges were pending. The round was subsequently taken to Camp Bullis, a military training area and firing range north of San Antonio, for safe disposal.The projectile was made for the Parrott rifle, a muzzle-loading rifled cannon developed by Robert Parker Parrott, a West Point graduate and inventor who became superintendent of the West Point Foundry. Parrott developed his rifled cannon system in the years immediately before the Civil War, with the first US rifled cannon of the design perfected in 1861. The weapon was recognisable by the wrought-iron reinforcing band around the rear of the gun, where pressures were greatest when it was fired. Parrott rifles were produced in several sizes and were used extensively by Union forces. The National Park Service records their use against Confederate-held Fort Pulaski in 1862 and Fort Sumter from 1863 to 1864.The Parrott system was significant because rifling gave artillery projectiles greater stability and accuracy than many earlier smoothbore weapons. Parrott also developed elongated projectiles designed specifically for his rifled guns. The combination allowed Union artillerymen to engage targets at greater distances and attack fortifications that had previously been difficult to damage. At Fort Pulaski, for example, Union forces used rifled artillery during the 1862 bombardment, helping demonstrate the vulnerability of traditional masonry fortifications to the newer technology. The National Park Service also records Parrott rifles among the artillery used during major Civil War operations, including the fighting around Antietam and the bombardment of Fort Sumter. The weapons became an important part of the Union's artillery arsenal during the conflict.After specialists confirmed the Texas relic was live, they transported it to an explosives range at Camp Bullis rather than attempting to preserve it as a historical object. The round was safely detonated there, bringing an unexpected end to an object that had survived from the Civil War into the modern era. Martin reportedly regretted that the relic could not be kept, but the incident changed how he viewed unusual military artefacts. The discovery also illustrates why apparently old battlefield ammunition can remain a serious hazard long after the conflict in which it was manufactured. Similar Civil War-era shells have been found in Maryland and at Gettysburg National Military Park, where bomb technicians have also safely destroyed unexploded ammunition. For Martin, what had seemed like an ordinary paperweight turned out to be a live piece of Civil War ordnance sitting in his home for years.
Article Summary: Steve Martin kept the Civil War-era shell on his desk for years as a paperweight. He thought it was a harmless dummy round until a military visitor examined it. Experts identified it as a live Parrott rifle, a Civil War cannon. It was later transported to an explosives range at Camp Bullis, where specialists safely destroyed it.

Article Title: Two young Minnesota farmers started grazing sheep under solar panels in 2017; their flock has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms
Article Text:
PC: North American Agrivoltaics Awards

How Minnesota farmers started solar grazing

How grazing-based vegetation management works

How the couple expanded the business

In 2017, Arlo Hark and Josie Trople founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, as a dedicated solar grazing operation. According to the North American Agrivoltaics Awards, the business has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms for developers, operators and owners. Its flock rotates across dozens of sites each season in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Iowa, with further sites in the western and central United States. The company offers Solar Grazing, Vegetation Management and Forestry Restoration, and has two sister ventures, Tethera and Bayl. The pair have been named the 2026 Solar Ranchers of the Year.Arlo and Josie founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, in 2017. It describes the business as a dedicated solar grazing operation that has now grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms for developers, operators and owners.The business started in the upper Midwest. Cannon Valley Graziers now rotates its flock across dozens of sites each season in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Iowa, and also grazes solar farms further afield in the western and central United States.The company's work now spans three service lines: Solar Grazing, Vegetation Management and Forestry Restoration.It describes Arlo and Josie as experts with applied experience in the field, who have combined these services into a single offering of grazing-based vegetation management.This approach costs less than mowing. It also builds soil health and biodiversity rather than simply suppressing growth, and it keeps working land working with natural systems. The citation says this operating model has earned Cannon Valley Graziers coverage from Bloomberg, Minnesota Public Radio and other media.Arlo holds a board seat at the American Solar Grazing Association. It says he shares leadership responsibilities with other board members and passes on the field-tested lessons that he and Josie have learned over the nearly ten years of building the business, which the citation says now has a footprint across the country.The couple have launched two sister ventures: Tethera, which focuses on meat, and Bayl, which focuses on renewable fibre. Both turn the flock's vegetation-management work into finished products, so that the business draws on food, renewable fibre and fashion, and grazing. Arlo and Josie, as younger farmers with a young family, say their experience shows that solar grazing can give the next generation of agricultural producers access to working land. It names land access as a problem that prevents many would-be farmers and ranchers from getting started.
Article Summary: Arlo and Josie Trople founded Cannon Valley Graziers in Northfield, Minnesota, in 2017. The business has grazed more than 6,500 acres of solar farms for developers, operators and owners. Its flock rotates across dozens of sites each season in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Iowa.

Article Title: A box of old games donated to a Texas Goodwill contained a rare 1982 Air Raid cartridge for the Atari 2600; Goodwill said only 13 copies were known at the time, and the game sold for $10,590.79
Article Text:
Representational photo of an Atari 2600 Game - SVG.com

Rare game goes up for auction

The 1982 Atari 2600 game "Air Raid" sold for $10,590.79 at a Goodwill auction. (Goodwill North Central Texas photo)

$10,000 sale to support Goodwill programmes

A box of old video games donated to a Goodwill store in Texas turned out to contain a rare 1982 Atari game that collectors had been searching for. The game, Air Raid for the Atari 2600, was sold at auction for $10,590.79 after a bidding war attracted 34 bids.According to Inside Edition,the rare find was discovered in early June 2021 at a Goodwill store in North Texas. Alex Juarez, an e-commerce item processor at Goodwill North Central Texas, was going through donated video games when he noticed one that looked different from the others.The game had a distinctive T-shaped handle and light-blue colour. Juarez recognised that it might not be an ordinary Atari game, so he called his father, who is a video game enthusiast. His father confirmed that the game was something special.The game was Air Raid, a title released in 1982 for the Atari 2600. It was manufactured by Men-A-Vision and was based on a simple premise in which players controlled an airship while defending Earth.Air Raid was not widely released. Its scarcity made it highly sought after by retro video game collectors. Goodwill North Central Texas said at the time that only 13 known copies of the game existed.The organisation did not know who had donated the game. According to Goodwill, the donor was most likely unaware that the old video game was a rare collectible worth thousands of dollars.After Juarez identified the game, Goodwill North Central Texas decided to put it up for auction rather than sell it through one of its regular stores.The auction began on June 10, 2021, on the ShopGoodwill website. It was scheduled to run for seven days, but interest in the rare Atari game grew quickly after it was listed.The first bid of $20 came just 15 minutes after the listing went live. By the end of the first day, the bidding had already crossed $2,000.The offers continued to rise during the following days. By the morning of the final day, the highest bid had reached $5,100.The listing attracted considerable attention from collectors. Goodwill said the game was added to 235 watchlists during the auction.The biggest jump came in the final minute. The leading bid increased from $6,300 to the final sale price of $10,590.79. The result surprised Goodwill officials, who had expected the game to sell for considerably less.Liz Confiliano, director of community engagement at Goodwill North Central Texas, said the organisation had looked at previous sales to estimate the value of the game. The most recent copy they could find had sold on eBay in 2011 for $3,575.The Goodwill copy did not have its original box, so the organisation expected it to sell in roughly the same range. Instead, the final price was almost three times the amount of that earlier sale.The money raised from the auction was also set to support Goodwill's community programmes. Goodwill North Central Texas said the more than $10,000 generated by the sale could fund day habilitation services for one adult with disabilities for a year. It could also support job placement services and community resources for 20 homeless people.The organisation said the money could alternatively help 10 at-risk young people earn their GED while receiving a paycheck.Rosemary Cruz, vice president of donated goods and retail at Goodwill North Central Texas, said the organisation was having fun with the unexpected discovery. The identity of the buyer was not disclosed.
Article Summary: The 1982 Atari 2600 game "Air Raid" sold for $10,590.79 at a Goodwill auction. Goodwill North Central Texas said at the time that only 13 known copies of the game existed. The money raised from the auction was also set to support Goodwill's community programmes.

Article Title: An $80,000 statue of an 1886 Kentucky Derby winner was stolen in California; thieves sawed through its legs and left one hoof behind
Article Text:
The 1886 Kentucky Derby winner behind the statue

The $80,000 statue became a Sacramento landmark

Thieves sawed through the bronze horse's legs

Only one hoof was left behind

Police are searching for the missing statue

An $80,000 life-size bronze statue of Ben Ali, the horse that won the 1886 Kentucky Derby, has been stolen from a road median in Sacramento, California. The nearly 7-foot statue had stood on Del Paso Boulevard for almost two decades and commemorated the horse’s connection to the city’s historic Rancho Del Paso. When the theft was discovered, only a single bronze hoof remained attached to the concrete base. Sacramento police are investigating the disappearance and have asked the public for information about the statue or those responsible. The theft has removed a distinctive landmark from North Sacramento and left behind an unusual mystery over how a large bronze horse was taken from a public location.Ben Ali won the 12th Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs in 1886 and became the first horse with a California connection to win the race. He was associated with Rancho Del Paso, a major horse-breeding operation in the Sacramento area. The ranch was established by James Ben Ali Haggin and became one of the most prominent thoroughbred breeding operations in the United States during the late 19th century. Ben Ali’s Derby victory became part of the region’s racing history and helped preserve the connection between the horse and Sacramento. More than a century later, that history was commemorated with a bronze statue on Del Paso Boulevard.The sculpture was created to honour Ben Ali and recognise his association with the historic Rancho Del Paso.The life-size bronze statue was installed on Del Paso Boulevard in 2007 and formally dedicated in 2008. It stood near the Sacramento Youth Center in the 1900 block of Del Paso Boulevard at Winnipeg Street. The sculpture was positioned on a concrete base in the road median and became a familiar feature of the North Sacramento neighbourhood. The statue was valued at approximately $80,000 and represented more than an artwork because it commemorated a specific chapter in the city's history. For nearly two decades, residents and people travelling through the area could see the bronze horse standing at the site connected to Ben Ali’s legacy. Its disappearance has now left an empty space where the historic monument once stood.The theft was discovered after the statue was removed from its concrete mounting. Reports said the thieves sawed through the bronze legs to take the horse, leaving one hoof behind on the base. The remaining hoof and severed section of the sculpture provided a visible indication of how the monument had been removed. Taking a nearly 7-foot bronze statue would have required considerable effort and some means of transporting the heavy sculpture away from the site. Despite the unusual nature of the theft, investigators have not publicly established a motive. It is also unclear whether the thieves intended to sell the bronze for scrap, resell the artwork or had another reason for targeting the monument. Police are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the disappearance.The theft has drawn attention because of the unusual scene left at the former location. Instead of finding the complete statue, people were left with the concrete base and a single bronze hoof. Images of the site show the severed section where the horse had previously stood, highlighting the scale of the theft. Community members have expressed disappointment over the loss because the statue was a visible reminder of North Sacramento’s connection to thoroughbred racing. The monument also carried historical significance because of Ben Ali’s connection to Rancho Del Paso and his Kentucky Derby victory. Replacing the sculpture would be expensive, with reports putting its value at around $80,000. The city does not have immediate funds set aside to replace it.Sacramento police are investigating the theft and have asked anyone who may have information to contact authorities. Investigators are working to determine who removed the statue and where it may have been taken. The Del Paso Boulevard Business Association has also drawn attention to the disappearance as community members hope the sculpture can be recovered. The case remains open and there is no confirmed motive for the theft. Until the statue is found, the single bronze hoof is the only remaining piece visible at its former location. What began as a monument to an 1886 Kentucky Derby winner has therefore become the centre of an unusual modern-day theft investigation in Sacramento.
Article Summary: Ben Ali won the Kentucky Derby in 1886 and became the first horse with a California connection to win the race. He was associated with Rancho Del Paso, a major horse-breeding operation in the Sacramento area. A bronze statue of Ben Ali was installed on Del Paso Boulevard in 2007 and formally dedicated in 2008. It stood on a concrete base in the road median and became a familiar feature of the North Sacramento neighbourhood.

Article Title: A Michigan collector paid $30 for a seashell painting at an estate sale; identified as a 1951 Gertrude Abercrombie work, it has now sold at Freeman's in New York for a record $1,352,600
Article Text:
Collector spotted signature at Michigan estate sale

Nine shells and one unusual detail

Who was Gertrude Abercrombie?

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Abercrombie's painting style appeals to you the most? Dreamlike imagery. Personal symbolism. Recurring symbols and motifs Unique subjects and themes. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A painting bought for just $30 at a Michigan estate sale has sold for $1,352,600 at auction in New York, after experts identified it as a long-lost 1951 work by Chicago Surrealist Gertrude Abercrombie. The painting, Alderman Merriam's Shells, had been missing from public view for about 75 years before it resurfaced this summer. It ultimately set a new world auction record for Abercrombie at Freeman's Post-War & Contemporary Art sale on October 1.The result was dramatically higher than the painting's presale estimate of $150,000 to $250,000. It opened at $80,000, with five telephone bidders and several online bidders competing for the work. Freeman's said the final $1,352,600 figure includes the buyer's premium; the hammer price was $1.06 million. The result made it the first Abercrombie work to cross the $1 million mark at auction.The discovery began at a Michigan estate sale in July, when a longtime collector of records and mid-century furniture was looking around after much of the merchandise had already been picked over. In a dark corner of a hallway leading toward the garage, the collector noticed a small painting measuring about 8 by 11 inches.The work showed a group of seashells against a subdued background. What caught his attention was the signature: “Abercrombie,” along with the year 1951.The collector paid $30 for the painting, apparently recognising that the name could be significant. He later investigated further and came across Abercrombie's retrospective, The Whole World Is a Mystery, which was touring the Midwest. The exhibition was presented at the Milwaukee Art Museum from March 27 to July 19, 2026 and brought together nearly 80 paintings from museums and private collections.The collector's research produced a remarkable match. The exhibition catalogue reproduced a 1952 Chicago Tribune photograph showing Alderman Merriam's Shells in its original frame, alongside the actual shells depicted in the painting. That archival evidence helped establish that the seemingly ordinary estate-sale painting was the same work that had disappeared from public view decades earlier. Dr Susan Weininger, an expert on Abercrombie and professor emerita of art history at Roosevelt University, subsequently authenticated it.Painted in 1951, Alderman Merriam's Shells depicts nine seashells arranged across a slate-grey surface. A conical shell appears suspended by a thread against a dark wall, giving the small composition an uncanny, almost floating quality. The shells were connected to Robert Merriam, a Chicago alderman who lived in Hyde Park, the neighbourhood where Abercrombie lived and worked.The work is particularly significant because it appears to show Abercrombie painting directly from physical objects rather than simply inventing them from memory. According to Freeman's, the painting provides evidence that the shells seen in some of her later solitary shell compositions were rooted in observation.The painting was exhibited in six solo shows during 1952 and 1953. Abercrombie later gave it to Dr John Reynolds of Kalamazoo, Michigan, in exchange for medical services. It remained with Reynolds' family for decades before eventually turning up at the estate sale.Abercrombie, who lived from 1909 to 1977, was a distinctive figure in Chicago's mid-20th-century art scene. Her paintings frequently featured spare landscapes and recurring symbols such as moons, owls, cats, doors and solitary figures. The Milwaukee Art Museum describes her as a leading figure in Chicago's Hyde Park arts community and notes her close connections with the city's bohemian and jazz circles. Musicians including Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker were among those associated with the gatherings at her home.Although Abercrombie developed a strong following among Chicago artists and collectors during her lifetime, she remained comparatively under-recognised nationally for decades. That has changed significantly in recent years, with museums and collectors paying increasing attention to her work.The 2026 Milwaukee exhibition was described by the museum as the most comprehensive presentation of Abercrombie's work ever organised. It was co-organised by Carnegie Museum of Art and Colby College Museum of Art and explored the artist's distinctive combination of dreamlike imagery, personal symbolism and Midwestern settings.The rediscovery also comes amid a broader reassessment of Abercrombie's market. The painting's final price at Freeman's was more than five times its high estimate and surpassed the previous auction record for the artist. Freeman's said the October 1 sale achieved $3,449,560 overall, with an 88% sell-through rate by lot and participation from buyers in 12 countries. The auction house also reported that 23% of its buyers in the sale were new to the firm.
Article Summary: Abercrombie's Alderman Merriam's Shells sold for $1,352,600 at auction in New York on October 1. The painting had been missing from public view for about 75 years before it resurfaced this summer. It ultimately set a new world auction record for the Chicago-based artist.

Article Title: A schoolteacher's 128-acre family retreat became part of a larger wildlife corridor; decades after buying the land, Jeanne Paisley's conservation easement now protects forests, wetlands and a stream l
Article Text:
A campsite she couldn't forget

A protected forest

When life doesn't give you time to breathe, you tend to look out for space to do the same yourself, deliberately. For Jeanne Paisley, a schoolteacher with three kids and a half-hour daily commute, there was a consistent wish for some room to breathe. According to The Land Steward, the Spring 2013 newsletter of the Finger Lakes Land Trust, Paisley had bought 128 acres of forests, fields and wetlands in the town of Richford in Tioga County, New York.It all began with a family road trip. Paisley and her husband lived on Long Island and had no summer work. Thus, the couple decided to buy a tent and took their three children on a trip all over the United States and Canada. When they returned to New York, they chanced upon this land and the family agreed it was the best campsite they had ever seen.The land suited her job as well. The drive to Paisley's school was just half an hour and she liked the setting. She recalled seeing red salamanders in the driveway when they first arrived at the site. And what made her especially glad was that there, no neighbour would ask her to mow her lawn. For her, the appeal was natural beauty and the freedom to leave nature alone.Paisley traced her love for the outdoors to her childhood during the Great Depression.When her father was unemployed, the family moved to the country. They built a small house and carried spring water up the hill. That early life stayed with her. In her words, "Caring about nature is just part of how I think." She added that she always knew she wanted to protect the land at some point. Decades later, she did just that.About 40 years later, at the age of 86, Paisley still continued to reside on the land. She had placed a conservation easement on her property with the Finger Lakes Land Trust. A conservation easement is an agreement that restricts the manner in which the land will be developed in the future.In this case, it was aimed at protecting the mature forests and prime farmland in the area of the east branch of Owego Creek. The Land Trust noted that two attorneys, John Alexander and Eric Haselbauer, provided pro bono legal help. This protection mattered because it helps safeguard the watershed. As reported in The Land Steward, David Diaz, the Land Trust's director of land protection, said the property helps maintain local watershed quality and supports fish such as eastern brook trout. He explains that because of its steep slopes and presence of a seasonal stream, the land is particularly susceptible to erosion due to stormwater runoff if disturbed by future development. Such damage can affect the water quality not only of the Owego Creek but also of waters many miles downstream. The property lies in a focus area for the Land Trust, where tributaries flow into the Upper Susquehanna River. That river's watershed drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the country's largest estuary.Andy Zepp, executive director of the Land Trust, said she and her family helped expand a network of protected lands in her Southern Tier neighbourhood. Her property joins several nearby protected areas, including multiple state forests, the Land Trust's King Nature Preserve, and another conservation easement.In a 2019 review published in Science Advances, Gregory Bratman and his co-authors summarise research related to nature and its impacts on mental health. Time spent in nature, the researchers argue, is linked with better well-being, better sleep, and lower stress. Many of the findings show links, not proof. Experiments suggest a short time in nature can brighten mood, but it is less clear whether that builds long-term mental health. The paper also lists water purification as one example of the benefits ecosystems provide, echoing Diaz's point about water quality at Owego Creek.
Article Summary: Jeanne Paisley bought 128 acres of forests, fields and wetlands in the town of Richford in Tioga County, New York. She placed a conservation easement on her property with the Finger Lakes Land Trust. This protection mattered because it helps safeguard the watershed. The property lies in a focus area where tributaries flow into the Upper Susquehanna River.

Article Title: She bought 3 Abbott shares for $180 in 1935; after her death at 100, her $7 million fortune went to help college students
Article Text:
Representative Image of Lake Forest College, showcasing students benefiting from a generous scholarship foundation (AI Generated Image)

How three Abbott shares became a multimillion-dollar fortune

Grace Groner's connection to Lake Forest College

How a modest donor left a multimillion-dollar estate

Why Grace Groner's story became a fundraising lesson

Grace Groner lived a modest life in Lake Forest, Illinois, despite eventually accumulating a fortune worth more than $7 million. She never married or had children, worked for more than four decades as a secretary at Abbott Laboratories and remained closely connected to Lake Forest College, where she graduated in 1931. When she died in January 2010 at the age of 100, she left her entire estate to a foundation benefiting students at her alma mater. Her fortune had grown from three Abbott shares she purchased for $60 each in 1935, an investment of $180 that she held for the rest of her life. Groner and her twin sister, Gladys, had been orphaned as children before the Anderson family took them in and helped support their education.Groner's extraordinary financial story began after she started working at Abbott Laboratories. According to the Grace Elizabeth Groner Foundation, she bought three shares of Abbott stock for $60 each in 1935. She held onto the investment and reinvested the dividends as the company continued to grow and its shares split over the following decades. The original $180 investment eventually became a fortune worth more than $7 million.Groner spent more than four decades working at Abbott as a secretary, but her lifestyle remained modest even as the value of her investment increased.She lived in a small one-bedroom cottage in Lake Forest rather than moving into a larger or more expensive home. Her attorney and longtime friend, William Marlatt, told contemporary reporters that Groner could have lived in any house in Lake Forest but chose not to. The precise value of her estate has been reported somewhat differently over the years. Contemporary coverage generally described it as about $7 million, while later accounts have cited figures around $7.2 million. Lake Forest College itself describes the gift as more than $7 million, making that the safest figure to use when describing the bequest.Groner's relationship with Lake Forest College began long before her fortune was known. She and her twin sister, Gladys, were orphaned when they were children and were taken in by the Anderson family of Lake Forest. The family helped the sisters attend boarding school and later supported their education at Lake Forest College, where Grace graduated in 1931.She remained involved with the college for decades after graduating. Before her death, Groner gave $180,000 to establish a scholarship programme intended to help students pursue internships and study-abroad opportunities. She also continued attending college events and maintaining a connection with the institution. Groner's charitable giving extended beyond the college. Contemporary reporting described her as someone who regularly made smaller donations to local causes, sometimes anonymously. Her lifelong pattern of giving meant that Lake Forest College knew her as a generous supporter, even though the institution did not know the full scale of her wealth.Groner had arranged for her estate to benefit Lake Forest College through a foundation. College president Stephen Schutt knew for more than a year before her death that she intended to leave her estate to the institution, but he did not know the eventual size of the gift. When Groner died in January 2010, the value of the estate revealed the extraordinary scale of the bequest.The Grace Elizabeth Groner Foundation was established to support qualified Lake Forest College students. Its current description says the foundation provides financial support to service-oriented students and helps fund service-learning opportunities in their communities, nationally and internationally. This includes opportunities that allow students to undertake service projects as part of their educational experience. Groner's former home also became part of her legacy. She left the cottage to Lake Forest College, and it became known as Grace's Cottage. The foundation says two female Lake Forest College seniors are invited to live there each year as Grace's guests. The cottage therefore became another way for her modest home to remain connected to the college and its students after her death.The size of Groner's bequest attracted attention in the fundraising world because her wealth was not apparent from her lifestyle. The Chronicle of Philanthropy reported on the case as a lesson for colleges seeking to identify potential estate donors. Fundraising writer Roger Craver pointed to characteristics in Groner's history that, in his view, could have indicated her potential, including her continued support for the college and her pattern of making smaller charitable gifts. Craver's interpretation should not be treated as a formula for predicting who will leave a large estate gift. What is documented is that Groner had maintained a long relationship with Lake Forest College, had given to the institution during her lifetime and had arranged for her estate to benefit it after her death. Her outwardly modest lifestyle did not reveal the value of the investment she had held for decades.Her story also emerged during a period when American universities were receiving a number of unexpectedly large anonymous donations. ABC News reported in 2010 that at least nine US universities had received gifts of more than $1 million from anonymous donors during the spring of 2009. The examples included an $8 million gift to Purdue University and a $6 million gift to the University of Southern Mississippi. Groner's bequest stood out because of the unusual path her money had taken. Three Abbott shares purchased for $180 in 1935 had grown through decades of holding and reinvested dividends into an estate worth more than $7 million. After her death, that wealth was redirected toward students at the college that had helped shape her early life, turning a quiet lifetime investment into a lasting source of educational support.
Article Summary: Grace Groner lived a modest life in Lake Forest, Illinois, despite eventually accumulating a fortune worth more than $7 million. She never married or had children, worked for more than four decades as a secretary at Abbott Laboratories and remained closely connected to Lake Forest College. When she died in January 2010 at the age of 100, she left her entire estate to a foundation benefiting students at her alma mater.

Article Title: Silicon Valley pioneer helped build HP’s first computer and collected wine for 60 years; 6,814 bottles from his cellar went to Christie’s auction
Article Text:
Image: Christie’s

Silicon Valley trailblazer who helped build Hewlett-Packard's first computer and began a wine cellar

Napa Valley renaissance : weekend visits to Ridge Vineyard and Joe Heitz when few Americans collected

Several important vintages from Heitz Cellar were offered in The Exceptional Private Cellar of a Silicon Valley Pioneer on 5 June 2026 at Christie’s in New York (Image: Christie's)

Early client of Kermit Lynch buying Bordeaux and grand cru Burgundy by caseload before prices soared

Rare Heitz Martha's Vineyard, Ridge Monte Bello 1974, Burgundy and Barolo standouts from the cellar

Single-owner provenance, impeccable storage and why this cellar was ahead of the curve for collectors

An original Silicon Valley pioneer who helped build Hewlett-Packard's first computer in the 1960s later became a venture capitalist and a key player in the modern renaissance of Napa Valley, according to Christie's. His private cellar grew to perhaps as many as 20,000 bottles, and after he died in 2025, Christie's was asked to sell the remaining 6,814 bottles. The sale took place on 5 June 2026 at Rockefeller Centre in New York. Chris Munro, Vice President of Christie’s Wines and Spirits, says every bottle has only ever had one owner and never left the cellar.After graduating from Princeton with an electrical engineering degree, the future collector drove from New Jersey to California in 1964, as the electronics and defence industries were turning Santa Clara Valley into a technology hub. Christie's reports that he took a job at Hewlett-Packard's Palo Alto headquarters, where he helped build the company's first computer.Around the same time, he bought a modest house in the rural town of Woodside, which decades later would be home to leaders of Apple, Sony, Intel and Oracle. Its cool basement soon began filling with wine. He went on to file multiple technology patents, co-found several start-ups and shape digital innovation as a venture capitalist.At weekends he made the hour-long drive to the newly established Ridge Vineyard, or to see his friend Joe Heitz, the pioneering vintner who was helping usher in Napa's modern era. He came home each time with cases of the latest vintages.Munro told Christie's that at the end of the 1960s very few people in the United States drank fine wine, let alone collected it, because the national taste ran to bourbon and martinis. Napa began to take off around 1968, and this collector was there at the very start.As his tastes widened, he became one of the earliest clients of the merchant Kermit Lynch, who opened his shop in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1972. He bought Bordeaux and Burgundy prolifically, at a time when great wines cost far less.Christie’s explains that a case of First Growth Bordeaux may now be worth ten times its 1970s price, and Burgundy has risen even more.
